The Iberian waterfrog, Pelophylax perezi, is a medium-sized ranid endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and southern France. Hatchlings emerge from their gelatinous egg masses following an incubation period of approximately six days [ab = approximately six days] when water temperatures are maintained at 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. At the moment of eclosion, these recently emerged larvae possess a wet body mass of about 4.2 milligrams [Wwb = about 4.2 milligrams], reflecting the modest yolk reserves contained within each 2 mm diameter ovum. This initial mass is remarkably low for a ranid of this ultimate body size, as adult females can attain a maximum snout-vent length of 8.6 centimeters [Li = 8.6 centimeters] in populations occupying productive Mediterranean wetlands. During the subsequent larval phase, the endotrophic tadpoles rely entirely on their yolk reserves before making the trophic switch to exogenous filter feeding on suspended algae and detritus.

After completing the aquatic larval period, metamorphosing individuals typically measure approximately 2.0 centimeters  in snout-vent length at the moment of tail resorption and terrestrial emergence. This transitional size shows some population-level variation, with a documented range of 1.7 to 2.2 centimeters, likely reflecting local thermal conditions and resource availability during the pre-metamorphic growth phase. At metamorphosis, the wet body mass of these recently transformed juveniles averages 0.82 grams , a value that scales allometrically from the adult size. Individuals reared at a constant temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] complete the entire larval development from hatching to metamorphic climax in approximately 70 days , a duration that is relatively rapid among western Palearctic water frogs. This relatively abbreviated larval period may confer a selective advantage in temporary or semi-permanent water bodies that are subject to seasonal desiccation across the species' Mediterranean range.

Sexual maturation in the Iberian waterfrog exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism in both size and timing. Females attain puberty at a snout-vent length of approximately 5.4 centimeters [Lp = approximately 5.4 centimeters], whereas males reach reproductive maturity at the smaller body size of about 4.3 centimeters [Lp = about 4.3 centimeters]. This size difference at maturity is consistent with the broader pattern observed across the Pelophylax genus, where females typically delay maturation to achieve a larger body size capable of supporting greater fecundity. In terms of mass at this developmental milestone, newly pubertal females weigh approximately 16 grams [Wwp = approximately 16 grams], a value that represents roughly a quarter of the maximum adult mass. The time required to reach this stage in females is about two years following metamorphosis when animals are maintained at a thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]; thus, female puberty occurs approximately 730 days after metamorphosis [tp = approximately 730 days after metamorphosis].

The maximum body size achieved by adult Iberian water frogs is not uniform across all populations, with some evidence suggesting geographic variation in asymptotic snout-vent length. In certain populations inhabiting less productive or more ephemeral aquatic habitats, the ultimate SVL is considerably smaller, with the largest individuals only reaching 5.8 centimeters [Li = 5.8 centimeters]. This reduction of approximately 2.8 centimeters compared to the 8.6 centimeter [Li = 8.6 centimeter] value recorded in high-quality habitats likely reflects constraints on the duration of the growing season and the availability of invertebrate prey. Correspondingly, the maximum wet body mass of adults in these populations is likewise reduced; the predicted asymptotic wet weight based on the larger ecotype is approximately 64.9 grams [Wwi = approximately 64.9 grams], calculated from interspecific scaling relationships with Pelophylax esculentus. Wild populations of Pelophylax perezi are also characterized by a considerable maximum lifespan, with the oldest documented individuals reaching an age of approximately 2,482 days [am = approximately 2,482 days] under natural thermal conditions averaging 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a longevity that is comparable to other medium-sized European ranids.

Fecundity and reproductive output in the Iberian waterfrog are strongly influenced by female body size and environmental temperature. At the average thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum annual reproductive output reaches approximately 5,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 5,000 eggs per year]. Females produce roughly 14 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = roughly 14 eggs per clutch] and can deposit approximately two to three clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately two to three clutches per year], reflecting a high potential fecundity for this medium-sized ranid. This reproductive strategy, combining a moderate clutch size with multiple clutches annually, is typical of many Pelophylax species inhabiting Mediterranean climates where the breeding season is extended but not unlimited. The interplay between adult body size and reproductive output is further underscored by the observation that the maximum adult wet weight of 64.9 grams [Wwi = 64.9 grams] is rarely attained before several years of growth, with smaller females producing proportionally smaller clutches.
